# Introduction

## Background

On **25 October 2026** Serbia held snap parliamentary elections. Three days before the vote, on 22 October, the polling agency **Ipsos Strategic Marketing** published its final pre-election estimate: the list *Aleksandar Vučić – Ujedinjena Srbija* at **47.4%** and the *Studentska lista – Studenti pobeđuju* at **40.0%**, with a stated 95% margin of about ±2.1 points for each.

The official count by the Republic Electoral Commission (**RIK**) turned that picture upside down: *Studentska lista* **53.0%**, *Ujedinjena Srbija* **39.0%**. Apart from the two large lists, only four national-minority lists (*manjinske liste*) entered Parliament.

A miss of this size, published by a long-established agency days before the vote and commissioned by one of the contestants, has raised a public question: **could a properly conducted random sample have produced Ipsos's numbers, if the electorate looked the way the official results say it did?**

## What this document does

We treat the official RIK result as the *true* composition of the voting population and ask how probable Ipsos's published numbers are as the outcome of a random sample of the size Ipsos reports. The natural mathematical tool for this is the **multinomial distribution**, which describes how a random sample splits across several categories (here: electoral lists).

The document is written for a reader without a statistics background. Every concept is introduced in plain language before it is used; every step is motivated before it is carried out and interpreted after. All code is included but hidden behind "Code" buttons, so the narrative can be read on its own. A compact, non-technical summary in Serbian is available as a companion document: [*Da li je Ipsos svoje brojke mogao dobiti slučajno?*](Ipsos-Izbori-2026-SR.html). Both documents and their source code are on [GitHub](https://github.com/GoranMilovanovic/izboriRepublikaSrbija_20261025).

## What this analysis can and cannot tell you

<div class="callout callout-warn">
**Read this before reading any number below.**

A probability calculation like this one tests a specific hypothesis: *"Ipsos's numbers are what you get when you randomly sample people who actually voted, and the only reason the sample differs from the population is chance."* If that probability turns out to be microscopic, the hypothesis is rejected: chance alone does not explain the gap. Throughout, the official RIK count is **taken as the truth**; the analysis says nothing about the count itself.

What the calculation **cannot** do is tell you *why* the gap exists. There are several candidate explanations, and a probability alone does not distinguish between them, nor between any of them and a combination:

1. **A genuine late shift** of opinion between fieldwork (20–22 October) and election day (25 October), which Ipsos itself flagged as possible;
2. **Differential turnout**: Ipsos predicted a turnout of 64.7%; the actual turnout was 69.0%. If the "extra" voters leaned heavily one way, or if some people who told Ipsos they would vote stayed at home while others who said they would not turned up, the population Ipsos tried to measure differs from the one that voted;
3. **Undecided voters**: Ipsos's percentages are shares of respondents who named a list. If the respondents who had not yet decided (typically a fifth to a third of a sample) broke very unevenly, the decided respondents were never a picture of the final electorate;
4. **Non-sampling error**: a sample that was random on paper but systematically missed or misread certain voters (telephone surveys reach some groups more easily than others; some respondents refuse or conceal their intention, especially in a polarised contest; the mix of telephone and online interviews, the question wording and the weighting targets all push results one way or another);
5. **Misrepresentation** of the published numbers, i.e. the figures not reflecting what the survey measured.

The honest shape of a conclusion from this document is therefore: *"Ipsos's result is inconsistent with random sampling error by such-and-such a factor; to rescue it, one would need a late swing of so many voters, or a turnout shift of such a size, or an undecided split so lopsided."* Section 9 puts numbers on those. Whether any of the explanations, or which combination of them, is plausible is a matter of judgement, of evidence from other sources, and ultimately of Ipsos's own transparency about its methodology. This document makes no claim about that.
</div>

# Setup

We use base R for the probability functions (`dmultinom`, `rmultinom`, `pbinom`, `pchisq`), the `pmultinom` package for the multinomial cumulative distribution function that base R lacks, and `ggplot2` for visualisation. The chunk below installs anything that is missing.

```{r packages}
needed <- c("pmultinom", "ggplot2", "dplyr", "tidyr", "tibble", "purrr",
            "kableExtra", "scales")
to_install <- needed[!vapply(needed, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(to_install)) install.packages(to_install, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
invisible(lapply(needed, library, character.only = TRUE))
```

theme_report <- function(base_size = 13) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "#fcfcfb", colour = NA),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#e1e0d9", linewidth = 0.4),
      axis.line.x      = element_line(colour = "#c3c2b7", linewidth = 0.4),
      axis.ticks       = element_blank(),

      plot.title       = element_text(colour = "#0b0b0b", face = "bold", size = base_size + 2),
      plot.subtitle    = element_text(colour = "#52514e", size = base_size - 1),
      plot.caption     = element_text(colour = "#898781", size = base_size - 3, hjust = 0),
      legend.position  = "top",
      legend.title     = element_blank(),
      strip.text       = element_text(colour = "#0b0b0b", face = "bold")

}

# ---- formatting helpers -------------------------------------------------------
fmt_n   <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",")
fmt_pct <- function(x, d = 2) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), x)
# turn a log10 probability into readable text, e.g. "2 × 10⁻³³ (about 1 in a 4 followed by 32 zeros)"
# (both halves describe the same number, each rounded to one significant digit:
#  p ≈ m × 10^f  and  1/p ≈ lead × 10^e; note that m is NOT the same digit as lead unless m ≈ √10)
fmt_log10p <- function(l10) {
  if (is.na(l10)) return("not computable")
  if (!is.finite(l10)) return("below 10<sup>−300</sup> (underflow)")
  if (l10 > -3) return(sprintf("%.4f", 10^l10))
  f <- floor(l10);  m    <- round(10^(l10 - f));  if (m == 10)    { m <- 1;    f <- f + 1 }   # p    = m × 10^f
  e <- floor(-l10); lead <- round(10^(-l10 - e)); if (lead == 10) { lead <- 1; e <- e + 1 }   # 1/p  = lead × 10^e
  sprintf("%d × 10<sup>−%d</sup> (about 1 in a %d followed by %d zeros)", m, -f, lead, e)
}
# a power of ten for prose, e.g. fmt_pow(-35.49) -> "10<sup>−35</sup>"
fmt_pow <- function(l10, d = 0) {
  s <- formatC(round(l10, d), format = "f", digits = d)
  sprintf("10<sup>%s</sup>", gsub("-", "−", s))
}
# integer counts for a poll of size n from published percentages (sum to n)
pct_to_counts <- function(pct, n, remainder_to = length(pct)) {
  k <- round(pct / 100 * n)
  k[remainder_to] <- k[remainder_to] + (n - sum(k))
  k
}
# log10 of a multinomial density, vectorised over the columns of a matrix
log10_dmultinom_mat <- function(X, p) {
  n <- colSums(X)
  (lgamma(n + 1) - colSums(lgamma(X + 1)) + colSums(X * log(p))) / log(10)
}
kable_report <- function(df, ..., align = NULL) {
  # text columns left-aligned, numeric-looking columns right-aligned; HTML (superscripts) passed through
  if (is.null(align)) {
    looks_num <- vapply(df, function(x) is.numeric(x) ||
                          all(grepl("^[-−+]?[0-9.,%× ]*$|<sup>|^$", as.character(x)) & !all(is.na(x)) & any(grepl("[0-9]", x))),
                        logical(1))
    align <- ifelse(looks_num, "r", "l")
  }
  kableExtra::kbl(df, ..., align = align, escape = FALSE) |>
    kableExtra::kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                              full_width = FALSE, position = "center")
}
```

# The data

## Why we need both sources on the record

The whole analysis rests on two inputs: what Ipsos published, and what the voters did. Both are reproduced here in full, with their provenance, so that anyone can check them and so that the document can be re-knitted when RIK publishes the final results.

## The Ipsos poll (published 22 October 2026)

Source: Ipsos Strategic Marketing, [*Rezultati istraživanja pred parlamentarne izbore – oktobar 2026*](https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Saopstenje_-_Ipsos_Strategic_Marketing_-_Parlamentarni%20Izbori_2026_-_finalna_procena.pdf) (PDF). The key methodological statements, translated:

- Fieldwork **20–22 October 2026**, sample of **3,624 respondents**; 90% telephone (fixed and mobile, random sampling), 10% Ipsos online panel.
- Representative of the adult population of Serbia **excluding Kosovo i Metohija and citizens living abroad**.
- The turnout percentage was computed on the whole sample. The **list percentages were computed among the "decided", i.e. respondents who said whom they would vote for**. The estimate **includes an assumed 2.5% of invalid ballots**, based on previous elections. (Consequently the 18 list shares sum to 97.5%.)
- Commissioned by the list *Aleksandar Vučić – Ujedinjena Srbija*.
- Expected turnout **64.7%** (62.9–66.5%).
- Ipsos adds: post-election surveys show that part of the electorate decides in the final days, so last-minute shifts between similar blocs are possible.

```{r ipsos-data}

ipsos_n       <- 3624
ipsos_turnout <- c(est = 64.7, lo = 62.9, hi = 66.5)
stopifnot(abs(sum(ipsos$ipsos_pct) - 100) < 1e-9)

ipsos |>
  dplyr::select(No. = no, `Electoral list` = list, Group = group,
                `Ipsos %` = ipsos_pct, `95% interval, low` = ci_lo, `95% interval, high` = ci_hi) |>
  kable_report(caption = "Table 1. Ipsos final pre-election estimate (base: all ballots cast, incl. an assumed 2.5% invalid). The 95% intervals are Ipsos's own; what they mean is explained in Section 6. Some list names are abbreviated.")
```

## The official results (RIK, snapshot of 31 October 2026, 11:00)

Source: RIK's [results portal](https://www.rik.parlament.gov.rs/542645/rezultati/) (Парламентарни → Парламентарни 2026), read on **31 October 2026 at 11:00**, when **8,339 of 8,392 polling stations** had been processed. These are therefore **preliminary** results; 53 polling stations (0.6%) were still outstanding. We also recorded the regional sub-totals for *Kosovo i Metohija* and *Inostranstvo* (polling stations abroad), because Ipsos excluded both populations from its sample and we will want to exclude them from the comparison too (Section 8).

<div class="callout">
**How RIK computes percentages.** RIK reports each list's share of **all ballots found in the ballot boxes** (valid + invalid), not of valid ballots only. This happens to be exactly the base Ipsos used (list shares plus an assumed 2.5% invalid). The two sources are therefore directly comparable without any rescaling (see Issue 1 in Section 4), with one subtlety we return to there: Ipsos's 2.5% is an *assumption*, not something its sample measured.

**Who gets seats.** A list needs 3% of the votes cast to enter Parliament; lists representing national minorities are exempt from that threshold (they compete under a "natural" threshold, with a bonus applied to their quotient when they are below 2%). That is why *Faktor stabilnosti* at 2.1% won no seat while four minority lists at 0.3–0.8% did. The seat figures below are the preliminary allocation at the same snapshot; they reproduce exactly from the vote counts with the d'Hondt method and those rules.
</div>

```{r rik-data}
rik_meta <- list(
  snapshot      = "31 October 2026, 11:00 CET",
  stations_total = 8392, stations_done = 8339,
  registered    = 6451292,   # all 8,392 polling stations
  turned_out    = 4433332,   # voters who were handed a ballot, at the 8,339 processed stations
  turnout_pct   = 68.98,     # RIK's own turnout figure (relative to the registered voters at processed stations)
  ballots       = 4430659,   # ballots found in boxes (valid + invalid)
  valid         = 4374187,
  invalid       = 56472
)

# national votes, in ballot order (no. 1..18)
rik_votes <- c(1726554, 94571, 2349777, 20415, 35004, 12132, 6492, 39485, 12562,
               12381, 20031, 2683, 1186, 4284, 2018, 3704, 27681, 3227)
stopifnot(sum(rik_votes) == rik_meta$valid,
          rik_meta$valid + rik_meta$invalid == rik_meta$ballots)

# regional sub-totals Ipsos did NOT sample: Kosovo i Metohija and abroad
kim_votes    <- c(25660, 1170, 7353, 13, 2, 10, 34, 360, 14, 12, 101, 6, 5, 23, 8, 10, 3, 7)
kim_invalid  <- 863          # 35,654 ballots at 2.42% invalid
abroad_votes <- c(19763, 386, 57756, 35, 17, 387, 29, 419, 278, 29, 78, 14, 3, 24, 11, 33, 8, 13)
abroad_invalid <- 304        # RIK 73rd session, 29 Oct 2026: valid 79,283, invalid 304
stopifnot(sum(kim_votes) == 34791, sum(abroad_votes) == 79283)

rik <- ipsos |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(no)) |>
  dplyr::select(no, list, short, group) |>
  dplyr::mutate(votes = rik_votes, kim = kim_votes, abroad = abroad_votes) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows(tibble::tibble(no = NA, list = "(invalid ballots)", short = "Invalid ballots",
                                  group = "Other", votes = rik_meta$invalid,
                                  kim = kim_invalid, abroad = abroad_invalid)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(rik_pct = 100 * votes / rik_meta$ballots)

seats <- c("Studentska lista" = 141, "Ujedinjena Srbija" = 103, "SVM" = 2,
           "Albanska koalicija" = 2, "Ljajić – Ljudski" = 1, "SDA Sandžaka" = 1)

rik |>
  dplyr::mutate(Seats = dplyr::coalesce(seats[short], 0)) |>
  dplyr::select(No. = no, `Electoral list` = list, Group = group, Votes = votes,
                `% of ballots` = rik_pct, Seats) |>
  dplyr::mutate(Votes = fmt_n(Votes), `% of ballots` = fmt_pct(`% of ballots`)) |>
  kable_report(caption = sprintf("Table 2. RIK preliminary results, %s (%s of %s polling stations). Seats are the preliminary allocation.",
                                 rik_meta$snapshot, fmt_n(rik_meta$stations_done), fmt_n(rik_meta$stations_total)))
```

```{r rik-summary}
tibble::tibble(
  Quantity = c("Registered voters", "Voters who turned out", "Turnout",
               "Ballots in boxes (valid + invalid)", "Valid ballots", "Invalid ballots",
               "Polling stations processed"),
  Value = c(fmt_n(rik_meta$registered), fmt_n(rik_meta$turned_out),
            sprintf("%s (RIK figure, relative to registered voters at processed stations)", fmt_pct(rik_meta$turnout_pct)),
            sprintf("%s (the %s voters who were handed a ballot but did not deposit one are the difference from the row above)",
                    fmt_n(rik_meta$ballots), fmt_n(rik_meta$turned_out - rik_meta$ballots)),
            fmt_n(rik_meta$valid),
            sprintf("%s (%s)", fmt_n(rik_meta$invalid), fmt_pct(100 * rik_meta$invalid / rik_meta$ballots)),
            sprintf("%s of %s", fmt_n(rik_meta$stations_done), fmt_n(rik_meta$stations_total)))
) |> kable_report(caption = "Table 3. Turnout and ballot totals (RIK, same snapshot).")
```

## Poll versus reality, list by list

Before any probability theory, the raw comparison. Each row shows where Ipsos put a list and where RIK found it. The two big lists are drawn on their own panel because they dwarf everything else.

```{r fig-dumbbell, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Figure 1. Ipsos estimate (orange) versus official result (blue) for every electoral list and for invalid ballots. The panels use different horizontal scales."}
cmp <- ipsos |>
  dplyr::select(short, group, ipsos_pct) |>
  dplyr::left_join(rik |> dplyr::select(short, rik_pct), by = "short") |>
  dplyr::mutate(panel = ifelse(short %in% c("Studentska lista", "Ujedinjena Srbija"),
                               "Two large\nlists", "All other lists\nand invalid\nballots"),
                panel = factor(panel, levels = c("Two large\nlists", "All other lists\nand invalid\nballots")),
                short = reorder(short, rik_pct))

cmp_long <- cmp |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(ipsos_pct, rik_pct), names_to = "source", values_to = "pct") |>
  dplyr::mutate(source = dplyr::recode(source, ipsos_pct = "Ipsos (poll)", rik_pct = "RIK (official)"),
                source = factor(source, levels = c("RIK (official)", "Ipsos (poll)")))

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = cmp, aes(x = ipsos_pct, xend = rik_pct, y = short, yend = short),
               colour = "#c3c2b7", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = cmp_long, aes(x = pct, y = short, colour = source), size = 3.2) +
  facet_grid(panel ~ ., scales = "free", space = "free") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "Where the poll put each list, and where the voters did",
       subtitle = "Share of all ballots cast. Ipsos, 20–22 Oct 2026 (n = 3,624) vs RIK preliminary count, 31 Oct 2026") +
  theme_report() +
  theme(strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0))
```

<div class="callout callout-result">
**What Figure 1 shows.** For each of the sixteen small lists and for invalid ballots, Ipsos was within about a point and a quarter of the result, and its estimates for the four minority lists that won seats (SVM, Albanska koalicija, Ljajić, SDA Sandžaka) were close. But the small misses all point the same way: Ipsos put nearly every small list, and invalid ballots, somewhat *above* their eventual share, so that collectively the small lists and invalid ballots were overestimated by about `r sprintf("%.1f", sum(cmp$ipsos_pct[!cmp$short %in% c("Studentska lista","Ujedinjena Srbija")]) - sum(cmp$rik_pct[!cmp$short %in% c("Studentska lista","Ujedinjena Srbija")]))` points. The bulk of the miss, though, is in the two large lists: Ipsos had *Ujedinjena Srbija* **`r sprintf("%.1f", 47.4 - cmp$rik_pct[cmp$short == "Ujedinjena Srbija"])` points too high** and *Studentska lista* **`r sprintf("%.1f", cmp$rik_pct[cmp$short == "Studentska lista"] - 40)` points too low**. One list deflated by thirteen points, with the difference spread over its rival and the small lists, is the signature we will be testing.
</div>

# Making the two sources comparable

## Why this step matters

A probability calculation is only as good as the correspondence between the poll's categories and the population's categories. Two issues have to be settled before we can proceed.

**Issue 1: the denominator.** Ipsos's percentages include an assumed 2.5% invalid ballots and therefore refer to *all ballots cast*. RIK's percentages are also shares of all ballots in the boxes. The bases match. (Had they not, we would have had to rescale one of them, which would have been a small but necessary correction: e.g. 47.4 / 0.975 = 48.6% of *valid* votes.)

There is a subtlety here that matters for honesty about the model. The 2.5% is a number Ipsos *assumed* from past elections, not a share its respondents produced; nobody tells a pollster "I will spoil my ballot". Under the chance hypothesis it therefore has no sampling variability at all, and treating it as if it were a sampled count (as the all-ballots base does, because it sits inside the "Other" category) slightly overstates how surprising Ipsos's result is. The actual invalid share was `r fmt_pct(100 * rik_meta$invalid / rik_meta$ballots)`, so the assumption was `r sprintf("%.1f", 2.5 - 100 * rik_meta$invalid / rik_meta$ballots)` points too high. We keep the all-ballots base as the main analysis because it is the base both sources publish, and in Section 8 we redo the key test on *valid votes only*, with the invalid share removed from both sides, to show how much that choice matters.

**Issue 2: how many categories to use.** A probability model with nineteen categories, most of them below 1%, is dominated by noise in the tiny lists and hard to read. The question of public interest is about the two large lists and, to a lesser extent, the minority lists that entered Parliament. We therefore define a compact **four-category scheme** as our main lens, and keep the full 19-category scheme as a secondary check.

## Scheme A: four categories

```{r scheme-a}
grp_levels <- c("Studentska lista", "Ujedinjena Srbija", "Manjinske liste", "Other")

scheme_a <- dplyr::full_join(
  ipsos |> dplyr::group_by(group) |> dplyr::summarise(ipsos_pct = sum(ipsos_pct), .groups = "drop"),
  rik   |> dplyr::group_by(group) |>
    dplyr::summarise(votes = sum(votes), kim = sum(kim), abroad = sum(abroad), .groups = "drop"),
  by = "group") |>
  dplyr::mutate(group = factor(group, levels = grp_levels),
                rik_pct = 100 * votes / rik_meta$ballots,
                rik_p   = votes / rik_meta$ballots) |>
  dplyr::arrange(group)

p_rik_A   <- setNames(scheme_a$rik_p, scheme_a$group)
pct_ips_A <- setNames(scheme_a$ipsos_pct, scheme_a$group)

scheme_a |>
  dplyr::transmute(Category = group,
                   `Lists included` = c("Studentska lista – Studenti pobeđuju",
                                        "Aleksandar Vučić – Ujedinjena Srbija",
                                        "SVM, Albanska koalicija, Ljajić – Ljudski, SDA Sandžaka (the four lists that won seats)",
                                        "The remaining 12 lists plus invalid ballots"),
                   `RIK votes` = fmt_n(votes), `RIK %` = fmt_pct(rik_pct),
                   `Ipsos %` = fmt_pct(ipsos_pct, 1),
                   `Gap (Ipsos − RIK)` = gsub("-", "−", sprintf("%+.1f", ipsos_pct - rik_pct))) |>
  kable_report(caption = "Table 4. Scheme A: the four-category comparison that drives the main analysis.")
```

```{r fig-scheme-a, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="Figure 2. The four-category comparison. Ipsos (orange) against RIK (blue)."}
scheme_a |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(ipsos_pct, rik_pct), names_to = "source", values_to = "pct") |>
  dplyr::mutate(source = dplyr::recode(source, ipsos_pct = "Ipsos (poll)", rik_pct = "RIK (official)"),
                source = factor(source, levels = c("RIK (official)", "Ipsos (poll)"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = pct, fill = source)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.62) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", pct)), position = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 3.6, colour = "#52514e") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = col) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%"), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Scheme A: four categories",
       subtitle = "Share of all ballots cast") +
  theme_report()
```

## Scheme B: all nineteen categories

For completeness we also keep every list (and invalid ballots) as its own category. This scheme is used in Section 7 as a robustness check.

```{r scheme-b}
scheme_b <- rik |>
  dplyr::select(short, group, votes) |>
  dplyr::left_join(ipsos |> dplyr::select(short, ipsos_pct), by = "short") |>
  dplyr::mutate(rik_p = votes / rik_meta$ballots)
p_rik_B   <- setNames(scheme_b$rik_p, scheme_b$short)
pct_ips_B <- setNames(scheme_b$ipsos_pct, scheme_b$short)
stopifnot(abs(sum(p_rik_B) - 1) < 1e-12, abs(sum(pct_ips_B) - 100) < 1e-9)
```

<div class="callout callout-result">
**Result of this step.** In Scheme A, Ipsos had *Studentska lista* at 40.0% against a true `r fmt_pct(scheme_a$rik_pct[1])`, and *Ujedinjena Srbija* at 47.4% against a true `r fmt_pct(scheme_a$rik_pct[2])`. The minority bloc (`r sprintf("%.1f%%", scheme_a$ipsos_pct[3])` vs `r fmt_pct(scheme_a$rik_pct[3])`) is essentially right. The residual category (`r sprintf("%.1f%%", scheme_a$ipsos_pct[4])` vs `r fmt_pct(scheme_a$rik_pct[4])`) is overstated by `r sprintf("%.1f", scheme_a$ipsos_pct[4] - scheme_a$rik_pct[4])` points; smaller than the two headline errors, but, as we will see, far from negligible in its own right. From here on, "the Ipsos result" means the four-number vector (`r paste(sprintf("%.1f", scheme_a$ipsos_pct), collapse = ", ")`) and "the population" means the vector (`r paste(sprintf("%.2f", scheme_a$rik_pct), collapse = ", ")`).
</div>

# The multinomial distribution

## Why we need a probability model

Polls are never exactly right, even when they are perfectly executed. If you ask 2,000 randomly chosen voters, you will not get exactly 53.0% for a list whose true support is 53.0%; you might get 51.8% or 54.3%. The question is never "did the poll miss?" but "**did it miss by more than chance can explain?**" To answer that, we need to know how much variation chance *does* produce in a sample of a given size. That is what a probability model provides.

<div class="concept">
#### Concept: the multinomial distribution {-}

Imagine an urn containing millions of balls in four colours, in exactly the proportions of the RIK result: 53.0% blue (*Studentska lista*), 39.0% orange (*Ujedinjena Srbija*), 2.2% aqua (*manjinske liste*), 5.8% grey (everything else). You draw *n* balls at random and count how many of each colour you got.

The **multinomial distribution** gives the probability of every possible count vector (so many blue, so many orange, …) for given *n* and given proportions. It is the direct generalisation of the coin-flip (binomial) distribution to more than two outcomes. A random-sample poll of *n* decided voters is, mathematically, exactly this urn experiment, with "true vote share" playing the role of the colour proportions.

Two facts about it matter here:

- The **expected** count for each category is simply *n* × (its proportion).
- The **typical spread** (standard deviation) of a category's count is √(*n* · *p* · (1 − *p*)). For a share near 50% and *n* = 2,000, that is about 22 counts, i.e. about **1.1 percentage points**. Random polls of that size therefore land within roughly ±2 points of the truth about 95% of the time, which is where the familiar "margin of error" comes from.

*Further reading:* Wikipedia on the [multinomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multinomial_distribution) and [binomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_distribution) distributions · the interactive [Seeing Theory, ch. 3 "Probability Distributions"](https://seeing-theory.brown.edu/probability-distributions/index.html) · Blitzstein & Hwang, [*Introduction to Probability*](http://probabilitybook.net) (free textbook; the multinomial is in ch. 7) · [Wolfram MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/MultinomialDistribution.html) for the formulas, including the covariance between categories. See also [References](#references).
</div>

## Seeing it: what random polls from the real electorate look like

The most intuitive way to understand the model is to simulate it. Below we draw 100,000 imaginary polls, each a random sample of 2,000 decided voters from the actual RIK electorate (we will justify the precise sample size in the next section), and look at the distribution of the *Studentska lista* and *Ujedinjena Srbija* shares they produce.

```{r fig-sim-intro, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Figure 3. Shares obtained by 100,000 simulated random polls of 2,000 decided voters from the actual electorate (RIK proportions). Histograms in each list's colour; the dashed line marks the true value, the solid black line what Ipsos published."}
set.seed(2026)
n_demo <- 2000
sim_demo <- rmultinom(1e5, n_demo, p_rik_A)
sim_df <- tibble::tibble(
  `Studentska lista`  = 100 * sim_demo["Studentska lista", ] / n_demo,
  `Ujedinjena Srbija` = 100 * sim_demo["Ujedinjena Srbija", ] / n_demo
) |> tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "group", values_to = "pct")

ref_lines <- tibble::tibble(
  group = rep(c("Studentska lista", "Ujedinjena Srbija"), 2),
  what  = rep(c("RIK (official)", "Ipsos (poll)"), each = 2),
  x     = c(100 * p_rik_A[1:2], pct_ips_A[1:2])
)

ggplot(sim_df, aes(x = pct)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(fill = group), binwidth = 0.25, colour = "#fcfcfb", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(data = ref_lines, aes(xintercept = x, linetype = what, colour = what), linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~group, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = col, guide = "none") +
  # the histograms carry the list colours, so the reference lines are kept neutral
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("RIK (official)" = "#52514e", "Ipsos (poll)" = "#0b0b0b")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("RIK (official)" = "dashed", "Ipsos (poll)" = "solid")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%"), expand = expansion(add = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "Share found by a simulated random poll", y = "Number of simulated polls",
       title = "What chance alone produces",
       subtitle = "100,000 random polls of 2,000 decided voters, drawn from the actual RIK electorate") +
  theme_report()
```

```{r sim-intro-range}
rng <- sim_df |> dplyr::group_by(group) |>
  dplyr::summarise(lo = min(pct), hi = max(pct), sd = sd(pct), .groups = "drop")
```

<div class="callout callout-result">
**What Figure 3 shows.** Across 100,000 random polls, the *Studentska lista* share never fell below **`r sprintf("%.2f%%", rng$lo[rng$group == "Studentska lista"])`** and the *Ujedinjena Srbija* share never rose above **`r sprintf("%.2f%%", rng$hi[rng$group == "Ujedinjena Srbija"])`**. Ipsos's 40.0% and 47.4% are not in the tails of these distributions; they lie far outside everything that chance produced in a hundred thousand tries. The standard deviation of a simulated poll's share is about `r sprintf("%.1f", rng$sd[1])` points, so Ipsos's figures sit roughly `r sprintf("%.0f", (100*p_rik_A[1] - 40) / rng$sd[rng$group == "Studentska lista"])` and `r sprintf("%.0f", (47.4 - 100*p_rik_A[2]) / rng$sd[rng$group == "Ujedinjena Srbija"])` standard deviations away from the truth. Everything that follows puts exact numbers on this picture.
</div>

# How big was Ipsos's sample, really?

## Why this is the crux

The probability of Ipsos's result depends enormously on the sample size *n*: the larger the sample, the smaller the chance of a given miss. Ipsos reports **3,624 respondents**, but its list percentages were computed only among the **decided** respondents (those who named a list), and the number of decided respondents is **not published**. Using 3,624 would overstate the precision of the poll and make our conclusion unfairly harsh.

Fortunately, Ipsos published 95% confidence intervals for every list, and a confidence interval is a function of the sample size. We can therefore **reverse-engineer the sample size that Ipsos itself was using** when it computed those intervals.

<div class="concept">
#### Concept: confidence intervals, standard error and effective sample size {-}

For a share *p* estimated from *n* random respondents, the **standard error** is SE = √(*p*(1 − *p*)/*n*), and a 95% confidence interval is roughly *p* ± 1.96 × SE. Turned around: if a pollster reports an interval of half-width *h* for a share *p*, the sample size implied by that interval is

  *n*<sub>eff</sub> = *p*(1 − *p*) / (*h* / 1.96)².

We call this the **effective sample size**. It can be smaller than the number of interviews for two legitimate reasons: (1) only part of the sample is in the base (here, the decided), and (2) weighting a sample to match population demographics inflates its variance; the inflation factor is called the **design effect**. A professional pollster's published intervals already incorporate both, so *n*<sub>eff</sub> is the right *n* to use in our multinomial model. Using it is also the **charitable** choice: a smaller *n* means more room for chance, and so a higher probability for Ipsos's result.

*Further reading:* Wikipedia on the [confidence interval for a proportion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_proportion_confidence_interval), the [margin of error](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margin_of_error) and the [design effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design_effect) · the interactive [Seeing Theory, ch. 4 "Frequentist Inference"](https://seeing-theory.brown.edu/frequentist-inference/index.html) for what a confidence interval really promises · Pew Research Center, [*Understanding the margin of error in election polls*](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2016/09/08/understanding-the-margin-of-error-in-election-polls/) · Zipf & Valliant, [*Design Effects and Effective Sample Size*](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/PracTools/vignettes/Design-effects.html) (the clearest free treatment of *n*<sub>eff</sub> = *n* / deff and of Kish's weighting formula).
</div>

## Backing out the effective sample size from Ipsos's own intervals

```{r neff}
neff_tbl <- ipsos |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(ci_lo), ipsos_pct >= 0.5) |>          # tiny shares are rounded too coarsely to be informative
  dplyr::mutate(p = ipsos_pct / 100,
                half_width = (ci_hi - ci_lo) / 2 / 100,
                n_eff = p * (1 - p) / (half_width / 1.96)^2) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(ipsos_pct))

n_turnout_eff <- with(as.list(ipsos_turnout / 100),
                      est * (1 - est) / (((hi - lo) / 2) / 1.96)^2)
deff_full <- ipsos_n / n_turnout_eff

n_primary <- round(median(neff_tbl$n_eff), -1)

neff_tbl |>
  dplyr::transmute(`Electoral list` = short, `Ipsos %` = fmt_pct(ipsos_pct, 1),
                   `95% interval` = sprintf("%.1f – %.1f", ci_lo, ci_hi),
                   `Half-width (pts)` = sprintf("%.1f", half_width * 100),
                   `Implied n<sub>eff</sub>` = fmt_n(n_eff)) |>
  kable_report(caption = "Table 5. Effective sample size implied by each of Ipsos's published confidence intervals (lists at 0.5% or more).")
```

```{r fig-neff, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="Figure 4. Effective sample size implied by each published interval. The solid line is the median, which we adopt as the primary n; the dashed line is the number of interviews Ipsos reports."}
ggplot(neff_tbl, aes(x = reorder(short, n_eff), y = n_eff)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = short, y = 0, yend = n_eff), colour = "#c3c2b7", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3.4, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = n_primary, colour = "#0b0b0b", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = ipsos_n, colour = "#898781", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.6) +
  annotate("text", x = nrow(neff_tbl) + 0.45, y = n_primary, label = paste0("adopted n = ", fmt_n(n_primary)),
           hjust = -0.05, vjust = 1, size = 3.6, colour = "#0b0b0b") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.55, y = ipsos_n, label = paste0("interviews reported = ", fmt_n(ipsos_n)),
           hjust = 1.05, vjust = 0, size = 3.6, colour = "#52514e") +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma, limits = c(0, ipsos_n * 1.05)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Implied effective sample size",
       title = "How many respondents do Ipsos's confidence intervals imply?") +
  theme_report()
```

<div class="callout callout-result">
**Result.** Ipsos's intervals imply an effective sample size of about **`r fmt_n(min(neff_tbl$n_eff))` to `r fmt_n(max(neff_tbl$n_eff))`**, with a median of **`r fmt_n(n_primary)`**. The two large lists, whose intervals are least affected by rounding, give `r fmt_n(neff_tbl$n_eff[neff_tbl$short == "Ujedinjena Srbija"])` and `r fmt_n(neff_tbl$n_eff[neff_tbl$short == "Studentska lista"])`; the smaller lists scatter more widely only because their interval bounds are published to one decimal place, which is coarse relative to their width. This is far below the 3,624 interviews, and it is internally consistent: the turnout interval, which Ipsos says was computed on the *whole* sample, implies *n*<sub>eff</sub> ≈ `r fmt_n(n_turnout_eff)`, i.e. a design effect of about `r sprintf("%.2f", deff_full)` on the full sample. Applying that design effect to a decided base of 60–80% of respondents gives `r fmt_n(0.6 * ipsos_n / deff_full)`–`r fmt_n(0.8 * ipsos_n / deff_full)`; the adopted `r fmt_n(n_primary)` corresponds to a decided base of about `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * n_primary * deff_full / ipsos_n)`, a plausible figure three days before an election.

We therefore adopt **n = `r fmt_n(n_primary)`** as the primary sample size. It is the figure Ipsos's own published precision supports, and it is the most generous choice for Ipsos. In Section 8 we repeat everything for a range of sample sizes, from a deliberately low 1,500 up to the full 3,624, to show that the conclusion does not depend on this choice.
</div>

# The probability of Ipsos's result

## Setting up the hypothesis

We now have everything needed to state the test precisely.

- **Population:** the RIK four-category proportions, **p** = (`r paste(sprintf("%.4f", p_rik_A), collapse = ", ")`).
- **Sample size:** *n* = `r fmt_n(n_primary)`.
- **Observed result:** Ipsos's percentages (`r paste(sprintf("%.1f", pct_ips_A), collapse = ", ")`), converted to integer counts out of *n*. These counts are a *construction*: Ipsos did not interview exactly `r fmt_n(n_primary)` decided people. The multinomial with *n*<sub>eff</sub> is the standard way of representing a weighted sample whose precision is that of `r fmt_n(n_primary)` simple random respondents; it matches the spread of Ipsos's own intervals, which is what matters for the test.
- **Hypothesis H₀:** the observed counts are a random draw from Multinomial(*n*, **p**).

```{r ipsos-counts}
k_ips_A <- pct_to_counts(pct_ips_A, n_primary, remainder_to = 4)   # any rounding remainder goes to "Other"
names(k_ips_A) <- names(pct_ips_A)
expected_A <- n_primary * p_rik_A

tibble::tibble(Category = names(k_ips_A),
               `Ipsos count (out of n)` = fmt_n(k_ips_A),
               `Expected under H₀` = format(round(expected_A, 1), big.mark = ",", nsmall = 1),
               `Difference` = sprintf("%+.0f", k_ips_A - expected_A),
               `In standard deviations` = sprintf("%+.1f", (k_ips_A - expected_A) / sqrt(n_primary * p_rik_A * (1 - p_rik_A)))) |>
  kable_report(caption = sprintf("Table 6. Ipsos's result as counts out of n = %s, against what the RIK electorate would produce on average.", fmt_n(n_primary)))
```

Already in this table the key quantity appears: the *Studentska lista* count is about **`r sprintf("%.0f", abs(k_ips_A[1] - expected_A[1]) / sqrt(n_primary * p_rik_A[1] * (1 - p_rik_A[1])))` standard deviations** below expectation and the *Ujedinjena Srbija* count about **`r sprintf("%.0f", (k_ips_A[2] - expected_A[2]) / sqrt(n_primary * p_rik_A[2] * (1 - p_rik_A[2])))` standard deviations** above it; even the residual "Other" category is about `r sprintf("%.0f", (k_ips_A[4] - expected_A[4]) / sqrt(n_primary * p_rik_A[4] * (1 - p_rik_A[4])))` standard deviations too high. ("Sigma" is shorthand for one standard deviation.) For comparison, a one-sided "2-sigma" event happens about 1 time in 40, a "5-sigma" event (the particle-physics discovery standard) about 1 time in 3.5 million.

## Why "the probability of exactly this result" is the wrong question

<div class="concept">
#### Concept: point probability versus tail probability {-}

With four categories and 2,000-odd respondents there are over a billion possible count vectors, so the probability of **any one exact vector** is tiny, even for the single most likely one. A poll that hit the truth to the decimal would still have a point probability of only a few in a hundred thousand. The point probability therefore cannot distinguish a well-executed poll from a badly flawed one.

The meaningful question is: **how probable is a result *at least as far from the truth* as the one observed?** This is a **tail probability**, usually called a *p-value*. There is more than one reasonable way to define "at least as far", and a careful analysis uses several and checks that they agree. We will use five.

One technical point: the probabilities we are about to compute are so small that ordinary computer arithmetic cannot represent them (anything below about 10<sup>−308</sup> becomes exactly zero). We therefore work with **logarithms** of probabilities throughout and report results as powers of ten: "10<sup>−30</sup>" means "one chance in a million million million million million".

*Further reading:* Wikipedia on the [p-value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-value) · Wasserstein & Lazar, [*The ASA Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose*](https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108) (*The American Statistician*, 2016; free access), the professional consensus on what a p-value does and does not mean · Wikipedia on [arithmetic underflow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_underflow), the reason for working in logarithms.
</div>

## Method 1: the point probability, for reference only

```{r m1-point}
log10_point_ips <- dmultinom(k_ips_A, prob = p_rik_A, log = TRUE) / log(10)
# (approximately) the most likely single outcome: the rounded expected counts
k_mode <- pct_to_counts(100 * p_rik_A, n_primary, remainder_to = 4)
log10_point_mode <- dmultinom(k_mode, prob = p_rik_A, log = TRUE) / log(10)
```

The probability of Ipsos's exact count vector under H₀ is **`r fmt_pow(log10_point_ips)`**. The most likely count vector (the rounded expected values, to within a count or two) has probability about `r fmt_pow(log10_point_mode, 1)`, i.e. roughly one in `r fmt_n(round(10^(-log10_point_mode), -3))`. Ipsos's result is therefore about **`r fmt_pow(log10_point_mode - log10_point_ips)` times less likely than the most likely result**. That ratio is informative; the raw point probability on its own is not, for the reason explained above.

## Method 2: one list at a time (binomial tails)

<div class="concept">
#### Concept: the binomial tail and the z-score {-}

If we look at a single category, say *Studentska lista*, each respondent either names it or does not, so the count follows the simpler **binomial** distribution with *n* trials and success probability *p* = `r sprintf("%.4f", p_rik_A[1])`. The tail probability "a count this low or lower" is computed exactly with `pbinom`. The **z-score** is the same information in standard-deviation units: (observed − expected) / standard deviation. For large *n* the binomial is well approximated by the bell curve, and a z-score of 3 corresponds to a one-sided tail of about 1 in 740, of 5 to about 1 in 3.5 million, of 10 to about 1 in 10<sup>23</sup>.

*Further reading:* Wikipedia on the [binomial distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_distribution) (section "Normal approximation"), the [z-score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_score) and the [68–95–99.7 rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/68%E2%80%9395%E2%80%9399.7_rule) that gives "sigma" levels their everyday meaning.
</div>

```{r m2-binomial}
binom_tail <- function(k, n, p, direction = c("low", "high")) {
  direction <- match.arg(direction)
  if (direction == "low") pbinom(k, n, p, log.p = TRUE) / log(10)
  else pbinom(k - 1, n, p, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE) / log(10)
}
m2 <- tibble::tibble(
  Category  = c("Studentska lista", "Ujedinjena Srbija"),
  direction = c("low", "high"),
  k = k_ips_A[1:2], p = p_rik_A[1:2]
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    expected = n_primary * p,
    sd       = sqrt(n_primary * p * (1 - p)),
    z        = (k - expected) / sd,
    log10_p  = purrr::pmap_dbl(list(k, p, direction), ~ binom_tail(..1, n_primary, ..2, ..3)),
    question = ifelse(direction == "low", "Share this low or lower?", "Share this high or higher?")
  )
m2 |>
  dplyr::transmute(Category, `Ipsos count` = fmt_n(k), Expected = format(round(expected, 1), big.mark = ",", nsmall = 1),
                   `z-score` = gsub("-", "−", sprintf("%+.1f", z)),
                   Question = question, `Probability` = purrr::map_chr(log10_p, fmt_log10p)) |>
  kable_report(caption = "Table 7. Binomial tail probabilities for the two large lists, taken one at a time.")
```

<div class="callout callout-result">
**Result.** Taken alone, the *Studentska lista* figure has a probability of **`r fmt_log10p(m2$log10_p[1])`** under random sampling, and the *Ujedinjena Srbija* figure **`r fmt_log10p(m2$log10_p[2])`**. Either one, on its own, is far beyond anything that sampling error produces.
</div>

## Method 3: both lists at once (the multinomial cumulative distribution)

The two lists are not independent: a respondent who names one cannot name the other, so a low *Studentska* count and a high *Ujedinjena Srbija* count go together more often than if they were unrelated. The proper joint question is: *what is the probability that a random poll shows Studentska lista at or below 40.0% **and** Ujedinjena Srbija at or above 47.4%, whatever the other two categories do?* This is a rectangular region of the multinomial distribution, exactly what the `pmultinom` package computes. (Technical aside: it uses a classical trick due to [Levin (1981)](https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1176345593), which turns an intractable sum into a fast exact calculation.)

```{r m3-pmultinom}
# pmultinom: P(lower < N <= upper); lower is exclusive, upper inclusive
p_norm <- p_rik_A / sum(p_rik_A)
joint_exact <- pmultinom::pmultinom(
  lower = c(-Inf, k_ips_A[2] - 1, -Inf, -Inf),
  upper = c(k_ips_A[1], Inf, Inf, Inf),
  size = n_primary, probs = p_norm, method = "exact")

# an independent check by brute-force simulation
set.seed(2026)
n_sim <- 2e6
sim_A <- rmultinom(n_sim, n_primary, p_rik_A)
joint_mc <- mean(sim_A[1, ] <= k_ips_A[1] & sim_A[2, ] >= k_ips_A[2])
# correlation of the two counts under the multinomial
rho <- -sqrt(p_rik_A[1] * p_rik_A[2] / ((1 - p_rik_A[1]) * (1 - p_rik_A[2])))
# given Studentska's count, where would Ujedinjena's count be expected to land?
us_cond_p   <- p_rik_A[2] / (1 - p_rik_A[1])
us_cond_exp <- (n_primary - k_ips_A[1]) * us_cond_p
us_cond_sd  <- sqrt((n_primary - k_ips_A[1]) * us_cond_p * (1 - us_cond_p))
```

```{r m3-table}
tibble::tibble(
  Approach = c("pmultinom (exact algorithm)", sprintf("Monte Carlo, %s simulated polls", fmt_n(n_sim))),
  `P(Studentska ≤ 40.0% and Ujedinjena ≥ 47.4%)` =
    c(fmt_log10p(log10(joint_exact)),
      ifelse(joint_mc == 0, sprintf("0 of %s (so below %s)", fmt_n(n_sim), fmt_log10p(log10(1 / n_sim))),
             formatC(joint_mc, format = "e", digits = 2)))
) |> kable_report(caption = "Table 8. The joint tail probability computed two ways.")
```

<div class="callout callout-result">
**Result.** The exact algorithm puts the joint probability at **`r fmt_log10p(log10(joint_exact))`**, and the brute-force check agrees in the only way it can: not one of `r fmt_n(n_sim)` simulated random polls from the real electorate came anywhere near Ipsos's combination. The joint probability is necessarily no larger than the rarer of its two parts (`r fmt_log10p(min(m2$log10_p))` from Method 2), and it is close to it: because the two counts are strongly negatively correlated (ρ = `r gsub("-", "−", sprintf("%.2f", rho))`; a correlation of −1 would mean one count always rises exactly when the other falls, 0 that they are unrelated), once a poll has *Studentska lista* that low, *Ujedinjena Srbija* being that high is no longer very surprising. In fact, given a *Studentska* count of `r fmt_n(k_ips_A[1])`, a random poll would put *Ujedinjena Srbija* at about `r fmt_n(us_cond_exp)` ± `r sprintf("%.0f", us_cond_sd)`; Ipsos's `r fmt_n(k_ips_A[2])` is `r sprintf("%.1f", (us_cond_exp - k_ips_A[2]) / us_cond_sd)` standard deviations *below* that. In other words, the votes Ipsos took away from *Studentska lista* did not all go to its rival; a sizeable part went to the small lists and invalid ballots. The correlation explains why the two headline errors travel together; it does nothing to make either of them plausible.
</div>

## Method 4: the exact multinomial test

<div class="concept">
#### Concept: "at least as unusual" measured by likelihood {-}

The most general definition of "at least as far from the truth" does not single out particular lists: it calls a result *at least as extreme* as Ipsos's if its **probability under H₀ is no larger** than that of Ipsos's result. The p-value is then the total probability of all such results. This is the *exact multinomial goodness-of-fit test* ("goodness of fit": how well observed counts match what a hypothesised population would produce).

How many possible results are there? A poll of *n* respondents split across four categories can come out in about *n*³/6 different ways: for *n* ≈ 2,000 that is roughly 1.6 billion count vectors. That sounds like a lot, but it is well within reach of a laptop: we can **list every one of them**, compute its probability, and add up the probabilities of those at least as improbable as Ipsos's. The result is exact, with no approximation and no randomness.

The textbook route is instead to *estimate* the same quantity by simulation, a **Monte Carlo** method: draw millions of polls from H₀ and count how many are at least as improbable as Ipsos's. Plain simulation has a floor: with two million draws it cannot see probabilities below one in two million. A standard refinement, **importance sampling**, is meant to remove the floor. Instead of drawing polls from the true electorate (where results like Ipsos's essentially never occur), it draws them from a *made-up* electorate centred on Ipsos's numbers, where they occur all the time, and corrects each draw by the ratio "how likely was this poll under the real electorate / how likely was it under the made-up one". We run both, and compare them with the exact answer: the comparison is instructive, because one of them quietly fails.

*Further reading:* Wikipedia on [goodness of fit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodness_of_fit), [exact tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exact_test), the [Monte Carlo method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_method) and [importance sampling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Importance_sampling) · Allen Downey, [*There is only one test!*](http://allendowney.blogspot.com/2011/05/there-is-only-one-test.html), a short, plain-language case that every hypothesis test is "simulate the null, count how often you beat the observation" · Jake VanderPlas, [*Statistics for Hackers*](https://speakerdeck.com/jakevdp/statistics-for-hackers) (PyCon 2016 talk; [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Iq9DzN6mvYA)), the same idea with worked examples.
</div>

```{r m4-exact-enum}
# The exact test by exhaustive enumeration: visit every count vector (n1, n2, n3, n4) with
# n1 + n2 + n3 + n4 = n, and add up P(vector | H0) over those no more probable than Ipsos's.
# One loop over n1; for each n1 the (n2, n3) grid is handled as a matrix, n4 being what is left.
exact_tail_enum <- function(k_obs, p, n) {
  thr   <- lgamma(n + 1) - sum(lgamma(k_obs + 1)) + sum(k_obs * log(p))   # log P(Ipsos's vector)
  x     <- 0:n
  a     <- lapply(seq_along(p), function(i) x * log(p[i]) - lgamma(x + 1)) # per-category pieces of log P
  const <- lgamma(n + 1)
  E     <- n * p
  tot <- corner <- 0
  for (n1 in 0:n) {
    m   <- n - n1
    idx <- 0:m
    lp  <- const + a[[1]][n1 + 1] + outer(a[[2]][idx + 1], a[[3]][idx + 1], "+")
    n4  <- m - outer(idx, idx, "+")
    ok  <- n4 >= 0                                      # n4 must be a count
    lp[ok] <- lp[ok] + a[[4]][n4[ok] + 1]
    sel <- ok & lp <= thr                               # at least as improbable as Ipsos's
    tot <- tot + sum(exp(lp[sel]))
    # the part of that mass in the "Ipsos-like" corner: Studentska below and Ujedinjena above expectation
    if (n1 < E[1]) corner <- corner + sum(exp(lp[sel & (idx >= E[2])]))
  }
  c(p = tot, corner_share = corner / tot, n_outcomes = choose(n + 3, 3))
}
enum <- exact_tail_enum(k_ips_A, p_rik_A, n_primary)
p_exact       <- enum[["p"]]
log10_p_exact <- log10(p_exact)
```

```{r m4-exact-mc}
log10_sim <- log10_dmultinom_mat(sim_A, p_rik_A)
n_as_extreme <- sum(log10_sim <= log10_point_ips)

# importance sampling: draw from an electorate centred on Ipsos's counts, re-weight to H0.
# The weights are heavy-tailed, so instead of trusting a single standard error we run
# several independent replicates and report the spread of their exponents.
set.seed(2026)
n_rep  <- 10; n_per <- 1e6; n_is <- n_rep * n_per
q_prop <- k_ips_A / n_primary
p_is_rep <- vapply(seq_len(n_rep), function(i) {
  sim_is <- rmultinom(n_per, n_primary, q_prop)
  l10_h0 <- log10_dmultinom_mat(sim_is, p_rik_A)    # log10 P(poll | real electorate)
  l10_q  <- log10_dmultinom_mat(sim_is, q_prop)     # log10 P(poll | made-up electorate)
  mean(10^(l10_h0 - l10_q) * (l10_h0 <= log10_point_ips))
}, numeric(1))
p_is       <- mean(p_is_rep)
log10_p_is <- log10(p_is)
is_spread  <- range(log10(p_is_rep))                 # exponents of the individual replicates
```

<div class="callout callout-result">
**The exact answer.** Enumerating all `r fmt_n(enum[["n_outcomes"]])` possible outcomes of a four-category poll of `r fmt_n(n_primary)` and adding up the probabilities of those at least as improbable as Ipsos's gives **`r fmt_log10p(log10_p_exact)`**. This is the headline figure of this document: the most general definition of "at least as far from the truth", computed exactly, with no approximation and no simulation error.
</div>

The two simulation estimates of the same quantity are instructive. Of **`r fmt_n(n_sim)`** simulated random polls, **`r n_as_extreme`** were at least as improbable as Ipsos's result. The plain Monte Carlo p-value is therefore **`r ifelse(n_as_extreme == 0, sprintf("below 1 / %s = %s", fmt_n(n_sim), fmt_log10p(log10(1 / n_sim))), formatC(n_as_extreme / n_sim, format = "e", digits = 2))`**, the resolution limit of this simulation, and consistent with the exact value. The histogram below shows where Ipsos's result sits relative to the two million simulated ones.

Importance sampling, re-weighting `r fmt_n(n_is)` polls drawn from an electorate shaped like Ipsos's numbers, gives **`r fmt_log10p(log10_p_is)`** (the `r n_rep` independent runs of `r fmt_n(n_per)` draws gave exponents between `r sprintf("%.1f", is_spread[1])` and `r sprintf("%.1f", is_spread[2])`). That is about `r sprintf("%.0f", 10^(log10_p_exact - log10_p_is))` times *smaller* than the exact answer, and the runs agree with each other far better than they agree with the truth. The reason is worth knowing. The set of results "at least as improbable as Ipsos's" is not a patch around Ipsos's numbers: it is a shell all the way around the true result, and it includes, for instance, polls that overstate *Studentska lista* by as much as Ipsos understated it. Only `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * enum[["corner_share"]])` of the exact tail probability lies in the Ipsos-like corner (*Studentska* below and *Ujedinjena* above expectation), and even within that corner the made-up electorate concentrates its draws near one point of a long ridge. Importance sampling is unbiased in theory, but in practice it almost never visits most of the shell, so it undercounts, and more draws do not cure it (we checked: a hundred times more draws moved the estimate by less than a third). We report it here as a caution, not as evidence.

```{r fig-m4, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="Figure 5. Log-probability (base 10) of two million simulated random polls under H₀. Ipsos's result lies far to the left of every one of them."}
tibble::tibble(l10 = log10_sim) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = l10)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, fill = "#2a78d6", colour = "#fcfcfb", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = log10_point_ips, colour = "#eb6834", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("label", x = log10_point_ips, y = Inf, vjust = 1.4, hjust = -0.05,
           label = sprintf("Ipsos*minute*s~result:~10^%.0f", log10_point_ips), parse = TRUE,
           colour = "#eb6834", fill = "#fcfcfb", label.size = 0, size = 3.8) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(c(log10_point_ips, min(log10_sim))), y = Inf, vjust = 4,
           label = sprintf("about~10^%.0f~times~less~likely~than", min(log10_sim) - log10_point_ips),
           parse = TRUE, colour = "#52514e", size = 3.4) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(c(log10_point_ips, min(log10_sim))), y = Inf, vjust = 6.2,
           label = "the least likely of two million simulated polls", colour = "#52514e", size = 3.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) parse(text = paste0("10^", x))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "Probability of the simulated poll's result (log scale)", y = "Number of simulated polls",
       title = "How unusual is Ipsos's result, measured by its own probability?",
       subtitle = "Two million random polls from the RIK electorate (Scheme A, n as adopted)") +
  theme_report()
```

## Method 5: the likelihood-ratio (G) test, which can reach the extreme tail

<div class="concept">
#### Concept: the G statistic and the chi-square distribution {-}

The classical textbook route to the far tail is an approximation. The **G statistic** (likelihood-ratio statistic) summarises the discrepancy between observed and expected counts in one number, G = 2 Σ Oᵢ ln(Oᵢ / Eᵢ). Under H₀, and for samples this large, G approximately follows a known distribution, the **chi-square distribution** with (categories − 1) **degrees of freedom** (roughly: the number of independent ways the counts can deviate from expectation; with four categories that must sum to *n*, three), whose tail we can compute analytically to any depth. Its close cousin is Pearson's chi-square, Σ (O − E)² / E; we report both.

Two honest caveats. First, the chi-square distribution is an **asymptotic approximation**: excellent near the centre, rougher the deeper into the tail one goes, which is why the G and Pearson versions below disagree by a few powers of ten even though they measure the same thing. Second, when they disagree in the far tail, G is the one to trust: its tail behaviour is governed exactly by the information-theoretic distance between the two vectors, whereas Pearson's statistic is known to overstate extremeness far out. We therefore treat Method 5 as a cross-check on the exact computation of Method 4, not as the headline, and read all of these figures as orders of magnitude.

*Further reading:* McDonald, *Handbook of Biological Statistics*: [G-test of goodness-of-fit](https://www.biostathandbook.com/gtestgof.html), [chi-square test of goodness-of-fit](https://www.biostathandbook.com/chigof.html) and [small numbers in chi-square and G-tests](https://www.biostathandbook.com/small.html) (the "expected count below 5" rule used for Scheme B), all written for non-statisticians · Wikipedia on the [G-test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G-test), the [likelihood-ratio test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Likelihood-ratio_test), [Pearson's chi-squared test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearson%27s_chi-squared_test) and the [chi-squared distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chi-squared_distribution).
</div>

```{r m5-gtest}
g_test <- function(obs, p) {
  n <- sum(obs); E <- n * p
  G  <- 2 * sum(ifelse(obs > 0, obs * log(obs / E), 0))
  X2 <- sum((obs - E)^2 / E)
  df <- length(obs) - 1
  c(G = G, X2 = X2, df = df,
    log10_p_G  = pchisq(G,  df, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE) / log(10),
    log10_p_X2 = pchisq(X2, df, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE) / log(10))
}
gA <- g_test(k_ips_A, p_rik_A)

# Scheme B: all 19 categories, merging those whose expected count is below 5 (the usual rule of thumb)
k_ips_B <- pct_to_counts(pct_ips_B, n_primary, remainder_to = which(names(pct_ips_B) == "Invalid ballots"))
names(k_ips_B) <- names(pct_ips_B)
small <- n_primary * p_rik_B < 5
k_ips_B2 <- c(k_ips_B[!small], `Small lists (merged)` = sum(k_ips_B[small]))
p_rik_B2 <- c(p_rik_B[!small], `Small lists (merged)` = sum(p_rik_B[small]))
gB <- g_test(k_ips_B2, p_rik_B2)

tibble::tibble(
  Scheme = c("A: four categories", sprintf("B: all lists (%d categories after merging %d tiny ones)", length(k_ips_B2), sum(small))),
  `G statistic` = sprintf("%.0f", c(gA["G"], gB["G"])),
  `Degrees of freedom` = c(gA["df"], gB["df"]),
  `p-value (G)` = purrr::map_chr(c(gA["log10_p_G"], gB["log10_p_G"]), fmt_log10p),
  `p-value (Pearson χ², less reliable this far out)` = purrr::map_chr(c(gA["log10_p_X2"], gB["log10_p_X2"]), fmt_log10p)
) |> kable_report(caption = "Table 9. Likelihood-ratio and Pearson chi-square tests of Ipsos's result against the RIK electorate (asymptotic approximations; orders of magnitude).")
```

<div class="callout callout-result">
**Result.** In the four-category scheme the chi-square approximation puts the probability of a discrepancy at least as large as Ipsos's at **`r fmt_log10p(gA["log10_p_G"])`**, within a factor of `r sprintf("%.0f", 10^abs(gA["log10_p_G"] - log10_p_exact))` of the exact value from Method 4 (`r fmt_log10p(log10_p_exact)`): remarkably close for an approximation this deep in the tail, and a reminder that the G statistic's tail is governed by the right quantity. Treating lists separately (Scheme B, `r length(k_ips_B2)` categories after merging the `r sum(small)` smallest) gives `r fmt_log10p(gB["log10_p_G"])`: the discrepancy is slightly larger in total (G = `r sprintf("%.0f", gB["G"])` against `r sprintf("%.0f", gA["G"])`), but it is spread over more than three times as many categories, and the chi-square distribution charges for each extra category. All of these agree to within a few orders of magnitude, which, at this depth, is agreement.
</div>

## All methods side by side

```{r methods-summary}
summary_tbl <- tibble::tibble(
  Method = c("Method 1 – Point probability of Ipsos's exact vector (for reference; not a tail)",
             "Method 2a – Binomial tail: Studentska lista this low or lower (exact)",
             "Method 2b – Binomial tail: Ujedinjena Srbija this high or higher (exact)",
             "Method 3 – Joint tail: both at once (exact; plain Monte Carlo)",
             "Method 4a – Exact multinomial test, exhaustive enumeration (exact; the headline)",
             "Method 4b – Exact multinomial test, plain Monte Carlo",
             "Method 4c – Exact multinomial test, importance sampling (biased low here; see text)",
             "Method 5a – Likelihood-ratio G test, Scheme A (chi-square approximation)",
             "Method 5b – Likelihood-ratio G test, Scheme B, all lists (chi-square approximation)"),
  `Probability under random sampling` = c(
    fmt_log10p(log10_point_ips), fmt_log10p(m2$log10_p[1]), fmt_log10p(m2$log10_p[2]),
    sprintf("exact: %s; Monte Carlo: 0 of %s", fmt_log10p(log10(joint_exact)), fmt_n(n_sim)),
    sprintf("<b>%s</b>", fmt_log10p(log10_p_exact)),
    ifelse(n_as_extreme == 0, sprintf("below %s (0 of %s)", fmt_log10p(log10(1 / n_sim)), fmt_n(n_sim)),
           formatC(n_as_extreme / n_sim, format = "e", digits = 2)),
    sprintf("%s (%d runs: exponents %.1f to %.1f)", fmt_log10p(log10_p_is), n_rep, is_spread[1], is_spread[2]),
    fmt_log10p(gA["log10_p_G"]), fmt_log10p(gB["log10_p_G"]))
)
kable_report(summary_tbl, caption = sprintf("Table 10. Summary of all methods, Scheme A unless stated, n = %s.", fmt_n(n_primary)))
# the range of tail probabilities across the methods that can reach the tail (the importance-sampling
# estimate is excluded: Method 4 shows it to be biased low)
tail_range <- range(c(m2$log10_p[1], log10(joint_exact), log10_p_exact, gA["log10_p_G"], gB["log10_p_G"]))
```

<div class="callout callout-result">
**Reading the summary.** Every method that can reach the far tail puts the probability between **`r fmt_pow(tail_range[2])` and `r fmt_pow(tail_range[1])`**, depending on how "at least as far from the truth" is defined (one list, both lists, or the whole vector) and on which approximation is used. The two that cannot reach it are consistent with that range: the *Ujedinjena Srbija* tail on its own (`r fmt_pow(m2$log10_p[2])`) is a deliberately weaker, one-list statement, and plain simulation stops at the floor of what two million draws can resolve, which is itself a finding: among two million ideal random polls, not one looks like Ipsos's. Our headline figure is the exact multinomial test by exhaustive enumeration, **`r fmt_log10p(log10_p_exact)`**, because it is the most general definition computed without any approximation; the chi-square figure, `r fmt_pow(gA["log10_p_G"])`, is the textbook approximation to the same quantity and lands close to it. The importance-sampling estimate is left out of the range because Method 4 shows it to be biased low. In substance: the hypothesis that Ipsos's published numbers arose from a random sample of the people who voted on 25 October, with chance as the only source of error, is not tenable. Sampling error alone cannot account for the gap.
</div>

## The same conclusion from Ipsos's own stated precision

There is an even simpler way to see this, which needs no model of ours at all, only Ipsos's own published confidence intervals.

```{r own-precision}
own <- tibble::tibble(
  Category = c("Studentska lista", "Ujedinjena Srbija"),
  ipsos    = c(40.0, 47.4), lo = c(37.9, 45.3), hi = c(42.1, 49.5),
  actual   = 100 * p_rik_A[1:2]
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(se_own = (hi - lo) / 2 / 1.96,
                outside_by = ifelse(actual > hi, actual - hi, lo - actual),
                z_own = (actual - ipsos) / se_own,
                log10_p_own = pnorm(-abs(z_own), log.p = TRUE) / log(10))
own |>
  dplyr::transmute(Category, `Ipsos 95% interval` = sprintf("%.1f – %.1f", lo, hi),
                   `Actual result` = fmt_pct(actual), `Outside the interval by (pts)` = sprintf("%.1f", outside_by),
                   `Ipsos's own SE (pts)` = sprintf("%.2f", se_own), `Distance in SEs` = sprintf("%.1f", abs(z_own)),
                   `One-sided probability` = purrr::map_chr(log10_p_own, fmt_log10p)) |>
  kable_report(caption = "Table 11. The actual result measured against Ipsos's own published margins of error.")
```

<div class="callout callout-result">
**Result.** Ipsos's interval for *Studentska lista*, 37.9–42.1%, says in effect: "an interval built this way would cover the true value in 95 out of 100 polls like ours". The truth was `r fmt_pct(own$actual[1])`: **`r sprintf("%.1f", own$outside_by[1])` points above the top of the interval**, which is `r sprintf("%.0f", abs(own$z_own[1]))` of Ipsos's own standard errors away from its estimate. For *Ujedinjena Srbija* the truth was `r sprintf("%.1f", own$outside_by[2])` points below the bottom of the interval, `r sprintf("%.0f", abs(own$z_own[2]))` standard errors away. By the precision Ipsos itself claimed, the chance of being this wrong on *Studentska lista* alone is about `r fmt_log10p(own$log10_p_own[1])`. A 95% interval is supposed to miss one time in twenty, and typically by a fraction of a point, not by eleven.
</div>

## The sampling cloud

One picture summarises the whole section (Figure 6). Each grey dot is a random poll of `r fmt_n(n_primary)` decided voters from the real electorate; together they show everything that chance can produce. Ipsos's result is marked, together with the box of its own published 95% intervals.

```{r fig-cloud, fig.height=6.5, fig.cap="Figure 6. Where ideal random polls land (grey cloud, 20,000 simulations from the RIK electorate), Ipsos's published result (orange), Ipsos's own 95% box (orange dashed rectangle), and the official result (blue cross)."}
cloud <- tibble::tibble(
  sl = 100 * sim_A[1, 1:20000] / n_primary,
  us = 100 * sim_A[2, 1:20000] / n_primary
)
points <- tibble::tibble(
