  sl  = c(100 * p_rik_A[1], 40.0),
  us  = c(100 * p_rik_A[2], 47.4),
  note = c("Official result\n(RIK, preliminary)",
           sprintf("Ipsos, fieldwork 20–22 Oct\n%s interviews, effective n ≈ %s", fmt_n(ipsos_n), fmt_n(n_primary))),
  # label positions: RIK below-left of the cloud, Ipsos to the right of its box
  hjust = c(1, 0), lx = c(52.3, 42.6), ly = c(36.2, 47.4)
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(lbl = sprintf("%s\n(%.1f%%, %.1f%%)", note, sl, us))

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = cloud, aes(x = sl, y = us), colour = "#898781", alpha = 0.15, size = 0.9) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 37.9, xmax = 42.1, ymin = 45.3, ymax = 49.5,
           fill = NA, colour = "#eb6834", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.6) +
  annotate("text", x = 42.1, y = 49.5, label = "Ipsos's own 95% intervals", hjust = 1, vjust = -0.5,
           size = 3.4, colour = "#eb6834") +
  geom_point(data = points, aes(x = sl, y = us, colour = who, shape = who), size = 4, stroke = 1.6) +
  geom_text(data = points, aes(x = lx, y = ly, label = lbl, hjust = hjust),
            size = 3.4, colour = "#52514e", lineheight = 0.95) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("RIK (official)" = 4, "Ipsos (poll)" = 16)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(x = "Studentska lista share", y = "Ujedinjena Srbija share",
       title = "Everything chance can produce, and where Ipsos landed",
       subtitle = sprintf("Grey: 20,000 random polls of n = %s from the RIK electorate. Each point is labelled (Studentska, Ujedinjena).", fmt_n(n_primary))) +
  theme_report()
```

<div class="callout callout-result">
**What the cloud shows.** The grey cloud, every result chance can plausibly produce, is a compact blob around the official result, about two points across. Ipsos's point is in a different part of the plane altogether, and its own 95% box does not come close to touching the cloud.
</div>

# Sensitivity: does the conclusion depend on our choices?

## Why check

Two choices in the analysis were ours rather than given: the effective sample size (Section 6) and the exact definition of the population (RIK's totals include Kosovo i Metohija and the diaspora, which Ipsos did not sample). A robust conclusion should survive any reasonable alternative for both. Here we vary them and watch the answer.

## Varying the sample size

We rerun the G test and the binomial tails for a deliberately low *n* = 1,500 (more generous to Ipsos than its own intervals justify), our adopted *n*, a "raw decided" *n* = `r fmt_n(round(0.8 * ipsos_n, -2))` (what the decided base would be if 80% of respondents named a list and there were no design effect at all; the 80% is an assumption, since Ipsos does not publish the figure), and the full 3,624 interviews.

```{r sens-n}
n_grid <- c(1500, n_primary, round(0.8 * ipsos_n, -2), ipsos_n)
sens_n <- purrr::map_dfr(n_grid, function(n) {
  k <- pct_to_counts(pct_ips_A, n, 4)
  g <- g_test(k, p_rik_A)
  tibble::tibble(
    n = n,
    `G test (Scheme A)` = g["log10_p_G"],
    `Studentska this low` = binom_tail(k[1], n, p_rik_A[1], "low"),
    `Ujedinjena this high` = binom_tail(k[2], n, p_rik_A[2], "high")
  )
})
sens_n |>
  dplyr::mutate(n = fmt_n(n), dplyr::across(-n, ~ purrr::map_chr(.x, fmt_log10p))) |>
  dplyr::rename(`Assumed n` = n) |>
  kable_report(caption = "Table 12. Probability of Ipsos's result for different assumed sample sizes.")
```

```{r fig-sens-n, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="Figure 7. Log-probability of Ipsos's result as a function of the assumed effective sample size. Every line is far below the conventional 5% and 1-in-a-million thresholds at every n."}
sens_n |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-n, names_to = "method", values_to = "log10_p") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = log10_p, colour = method)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = log10(0.05), linetype = "dotted", colour = "#898781") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -6, linetype = "dotted", colour = "#898781") +
  annotate("text", x = 1500, y = log10(0.05), label = "p = 0.05", hjust = 0, vjust = -0.5, size = 3.6, colour = "#52514e") +
  annotate("text", x = 1500, y = -6, label = "p = one in a million", hjust = 0, vjust = -0.5, size = 3.6, colour = "#52514e") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("G test (Scheme A)" = "#0b0b0b", "Studentska this low" = "#2a78d6", "Ujedinjena this high" = "#eb6834")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = n_grid, labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) parse(text = paste0("10^", x)), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.1))) +
  labs(x = "Assumed effective sample size", y = "Probability under random sampling",
       title = "The conclusion does not depend on the sample size we assume") +
  theme_report()
```

## Varying the population: excluding Kosovo i Metohija and the diaspora

Ipsos surveyed only citizens present in Serbia without Kosovo i Metohija. Voters abroad broke overwhelmingly for *Studentska lista* (`r fmt_pct(100 * abroad_votes[3] / sum(abroad_votes), 1)` of their valid votes), voters in Kosovo i Metohija overwhelmingly for *Ujedinjena Srbija* (`r fmt_pct(100 * kim_votes[1] / sum(kim_votes), 1)`). The fair comparison removes both from the population.

```{r sens-pop}
scheme_a_adj <- scheme_a |>
  dplyr::mutate(votes_adj = votes - kim - abroad,
                rik_p_adj = votes_adj / sum(votes_adj),
                rik_pct_adj = 100 * rik_p_adj)
p_rik_A_adj <- setNames(scheme_a_adj$rik_p_adj, scheme_a_adj$group)
g_adj  <- g_test(k_ips_A, p_rik_A_adj)
bin_adj <- c(binom_tail(k_ips_A[1], n_primary, p_rik_A_adj[1], "low"),
             binom_tail(k_ips_A[2], n_primary, p_rik_A_adj[2], "high"))

scheme_a_adj |>
  dplyr::transmute(Category = group, `RIK % (all voters)` = fmt_pct(rik_pct),
                   `RIK % (Serbia proper, without Kosovo i Metohija and abroad)` = fmt_pct(rik_pct_adj),
                   `Ipsos %` = fmt_pct(ipsos_pct, 1)) |>
  kable_report(caption = sprintf("Table 13. The population redefined to match Ipsos's sampling frame (removes %s ballots).",
                                 fmt_n(sum(scheme_a$kim + scheme_a$abroad))))
```

<div class="callout callout-result">
**Result.** Matching Ipsos's sampling frame moves the *Studentska lista* share from `r fmt_pct(scheme_a$rik_pct[1])` to `r fmt_pct(scheme_a_adj$rik_pct_adj[1])` and *Ujedinjena Srbija* from `r fmt_pct(scheme_a$rik_pct[2])` to `r fmt_pct(scheme_a_adj$rik_pct_adj[2])`: changes in the second decimal, because the two excluded populations are small and pull in opposite directions. The G-test probability rises slightly, from `r fmt_log10p(gA["log10_p_G"])` to `r fmt_log10p(g_adj["log10_p_G"])`. The population definition is not the explanation.
</div>

## Varying the base: valid votes only

As explained in Section 4 (Issue 1), Ipsos's 2.5% invalid share is an assumption rather than a measurement, so it should not really be allowed to count as "sampling evidence". Here we remove invalid ballots from both sides: Ipsos's list shares are rescaled to the 97.5% that its respondents actually produced, and RIK's shares are taken over valid votes. This is the fairest version of the test for Ipsos.

```{r sens-valid}
# Scheme A on the valid-vote base: drop the invalid row from both sources
ips_valid <- ipsos |> dplyr::filter(short != "Invalid ballots") |>
  dplyr::group_by(group) |> dplyr::summarise(pct = sum(ipsos_pct) / 0.975, .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(group = factor(group, levels = grp_levels)) |> dplyr::arrange(group)
rik_valid <- rik |> dplyr::filter(short != "Invalid ballots") |>
  dplyr::group_by(group) |> dplyr::summarise(votes = sum(votes), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(group = factor(group, levels = grp_levels)) |> dplyr::arrange(group)
p_rik_A_valid   <- setNames(rik_valid$votes / sum(rik_valid$votes), grp_levels)
pct_ips_A_valid <- setNames(ips_valid$pct, grp_levels)
k_ips_A_valid   <- pct_to_counts(pct_ips_A_valid, n_primary, 4)
g_valid   <- g_test(k_ips_A_valid, p_rik_A_valid)
bin_valid <- binom_tail(k_ips_A_valid[1], n_primary, p_rik_A_valid[1], "low")

# Scheme B on the valid-vote base
sb_valid <- scheme_b |> dplyr::filter(short != "Invalid ballots") |>
  dplyr::mutate(p = votes / sum(votes), pct = ipsos_pct / 0.975)
k_B_valid <- pct_to_counts(sb_valid$pct, n_primary, which.max(sb_valid$pct)); names(k_B_valid) <- sb_valid$short
p_B_valid <- setNames(sb_valid$p, sb_valid$short)
small_v   <- n_primary * p_B_valid < 5
k_B_valid2 <- c(k_B_valid[!small_v], `Small lists (merged)` = sum(k_B_valid[small_v]))
p_B_valid2 <- c(p_B_valid[!small_v], `Small lists (merged)` = sum(p_B_valid[small_v]))
gB_valid <- g_test(k_B_valid2, p_B_valid2)

tibble::tibble(
  Test = c("Studentska lista this low or lower (binomial)", "G test, Scheme A", "G test, Scheme B"),
  `All ballots (main analysis)` = purrr::map_chr(c(m2$log10_p[1], gA["log10_p_G"], gB["log10_p_G"]), fmt_log10p),
  `Valid votes only` = purrr::map_chr(c(bin_valid, g_valid["log10_p_G"], gB_valid["log10_p_G"]), fmt_log10p)
) |> kable_report(caption = "Table 14. The key tests with invalid ballots removed from both sources.")
# the overall range of tail probabilities across methods AND bases, used in the conclusions
tail_range_all <- range(c(tail_range, g_valid["log10_p_G"], gB_valid["log10_p_G"]))
```

<div class="callout callout-result">
**Result.** On the valid-vote base *Studentska lista*'s true share is `r fmt_pct(100 * p_rik_A_valid[1])` and Ipsos's rescaled estimate `r sprintf("%.1f%%", pct_ips_A_valid[1])`; the gap narrows by a fraction of a point and the "Other" category loses the 1.2-point invalid-ballot overestimate. The probabilities move accordingly: the Scheme A test from `r fmt_pow(gA["log10_p_G"])` to `r fmt_pow(g_valid["log10_p_G"])`, Scheme B from `r fmt_pow(gB["log10_p_G"])` to `r fmt_pow(gB_valid["log10_p_G"])`. Three or four powers of ten is a real difference, and it is the reason this document reports its headline as an order of magnitude rather than a precise figure. It does not come close to changing the conclusion.

Across every combination of sample size, population definition and base, the probability of Ipsos's result under random sampling never rises above about `r fmt_pow(max(c(sens_n[["G test (Scheme A)"]], g_valid["log10_p_G"], gB_valid["log10_p_G"])))`. The conclusion of Section 7 is not an artefact of our choices.
</div>

# What would it take to rescue the poll?

## Why ask

A probability of `r fmt_pow(log10_p_exact)` is not a number anyone can feel. A more useful way to express the same finding is to ask: **how large would each innocent explanation have to be to make Ipsos's result ordinary?** This section quantifies the three explanations that concern the electorate rather than the pollster's instrument: a genuine late swing of opinion, differential turnout, and the behaviour of undecided voters.

## Scenario 1: a late swing between 22 and 25 October

Suppose the electorate on 22 October was closer to Ipsos's picture than the final result shows, and that voters then moved in the final three days. How many would have had to move for Ipsos's result to have been merely unlucky, i.e. to have had a 5% probability, the conventional border of "could be chance"?

Ipsos's picture differs from the result in all four categories (too few *Studentska* voters, too many *Ujedinjena Srbija* voters, and too many voters for the small lists and invalid ballots), so the cleanest way to pose the question is this: suppose the electorate on 22 October was somewhere **on the straight line between Ipsos's picture and the actual result**, and then drifted towards the actual result by election day. How far along that line towards Ipsos's picture would the electorate have had to be for Ipsos's poll to have had a 5% probability? We express the answer as the number of voters who would then have had to switch **to *Studentska lista*** in the final three days. Moving along this particular line is also the direction that needs the *fewest* movers (any swing that left the small-list excess in place could never rescue the poll), so the figure below is a lower bound, i.e. the most generous answer for Ipsos.

```{r swing}
p_ips_A <- pct_ips_A / 100
# population a fraction t of the way from the actual result towards Ipsos's picture
swing_log10p <- function(t, k = k_ips_A, p_from = p_rik_A, p_to = p_ips_A) {
  p2 <- (1 - t) * p_from + t * p_to
  g_test(k, p2)["log10_p_G"]
}
t_05 <- uniroot(function(t) swing_log10p(t) - log10(0.05), c(0, 1))$root
t_50 <- uniroot(function(t) swing_log10p(t) - log10(0.50), c(0, 1))$root
to_sl <- function(t) t * (p_rik_A[1] - p_ips_A[1]) * rik_meta$ballots       # voters who must move TO Studentska
from_us <- function(t) t * (p_ips_A[2] - p_rik_A[2]) * rik_meta$ballots     # ... of whom from Ujedinjena Srbija
voters_05 <- to_sl(t_05); voters_50 <- to_sl(t_50)

swing_df <- tibble::tibble(t = seq(0, 1, by = 0.01)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(voters = to_sl(t), log10_p = purrr::map_dbl(t, swing_log10p))

# how much does the answer depend on the assumed sample size?
voters_05_by_n <- vapply(n_grid, function(n) {
  k <- pct_to_counts(pct_ips_A, n, 4)
  to_sl(uniroot(function(t) swing_log10p(t, k = k) - log10(0.05), c(0, 1))$root)
}, numeric(1))
```

```{r fig-swing, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="Figure 8. How the probability of Ipsos's result rises as we assume ever more voters moved to Studentska lista after the poll (the electorate drifting from Ipsos's picture towards the actual result)."}
ggplot(swing_df, aes(x = voters, y = log10_p)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = log10(0.05), linetype = "dotted", colour = "#898781") +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = log10(0.05), label = "p = 0.05 (“could be chance”)", hjust = 0, vjust = -0.5, size = 3.6, colour = "#52514e") +
  geom_line(colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = voters_05, colour = "#eb6834", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("label", x = voters_05, y = min(swing_df$log10_p) * 0.5,
           label = sprintf("about %s voters\nwould have had to move\nto Studentska lista", fmt_n(round(voters_05, -3))),
           hjust = 1.05, size = 3.5, colour = "#eb6834", fill = "#fcfcfb", label.size = 0) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.08))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) parse(text = paste0("10^", x)), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.1))) +
  labs(x = "Voters assumed to have moved to Studentska lista between 22 and 25 October",
       y = "Probability of Ipsos's result", title = "Scenario 1: how big a late swing would rescue the poll?") +
  theme_report()
```

<div class="callout callout-result">
**Result.** For Ipsos's result to have been merely a 1-in-20 unlucky draw, the electorate on 22 October would have had to be **`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * t_05)`% of the way** from the actual result to Ipsos's picture, which means that about **`r fmt_n(round(voters_05, -3))` voters** (`r fmt_pct(100 * voters_05 / rik_meta$ballots, 1)` of all ballots cast) would have had to move to *Studentska lista* in the three days after the fieldwork, roughly `r fmt_n(round(from_us(t_05), -3))` of them from *Ujedinjena Srbija* and the rest voters who would otherwise have backed a small list or cast an invalid ballot. (The figure depends a little on the assumed sample size: between `r fmt_n(round(min(voters_05_by_n), -3))` and `r fmt_n(round(max(voters_05_by_n), -3))` across the range of *n* used in Section 8.) For Ipsos's poll to have been a typical, median poll, about `r fmt_n(round(voters_50, -3))` voters would have had to move. That is a swing of some `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * voters_05 / rik_meta$ballots)` points within 72 hours, in an election where no event of that magnitude was reported between 22 and 25 October; it would mean *Ujedinjena Srbija* losing about one in `r sprintf("%.0f", 1 / (from_us(t_05) / (p_rik_A[2] * rik_meta$ballots + from_us(t_05))))` of its 22-October supporters by polling day. Late swings of one to three points are common in the polling literature; a swing of this size within three days is, to our knowledge, undocumented in comparable elections. (For what polling error normally looks like across 351 elections in 45 countries, see [Jennings & Wlezien, 2018](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-018-0315-6); for a forensic account of an unusually bad polling year and why non-response rather than late swing or turnout models was the likely cause, see the [AAPOR Task Force report on 2020 U.S. pre-election polls](https://aapor.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/AAPOR-Task-Force-on-2020-Pre-Election-Polling_Report-FNL.pdf).)
</div>

## Scenario 2: differential turnout (the net surplus)

Ipsos predicted a turnout of `r ipsos_turnout["est"]`%; actual turnout was `r fmt_pct(rik_meta$turnout_pct)`. The difference is about **`r fmt_n(round((rik_meta$turnout_pct - ipsos_turnout["est"]) / 100 * rik_meta$turned_out / (rik_meta$turnout_pct / 100), -3))` voters** who turned out but whom Ipsos's model expected to stay home. (The two percentages have slightly different bases, Ipsos's being adults in Serbia proper and RIK's registered voters including Kosovo i Metohija and abroad, so this is an approximation; the scenario is deliberately extreme in any case.) Could these "unexpected" voters account for the gap? We take the extreme case for this *net* surplus: **every single one of them voted for *Studentska lista***. Removing them from the count gives the electorate Ipsos thought it was measuring.

```{r turnout}
registered_processed <- rik_meta$turned_out / (rik_meta$turnout_pct / 100)       # registered voters at the processed stations
extra_voters <- (rik_meta$turnout_pct - ipsos_turnout["est"]) / 100 * registered_processed
votes_t <- scheme_a$votes
votes_t[1] <- votes_t[1] - extra_voters                      # all extra voters assumed to be Studentska voters
p_turnout <- votes_t / sum(votes_t)
g_turn <- g_test(k_ips_A, p_turnout)

tibble::tibble(Category = scheme_a$group,
               `RIK % (actual)` = fmt_pct(100 * p_rik_A),
               `% if all extra turnout were Studentska voters` = fmt_pct(100 * p_turnout),
               `Ipsos %` = fmt_pct(pct_ips_A, 1)) |>
  kable_report(caption = sprintf("Table 15. Scenario 2: the electorate Ipsos expected, under the extreme assumption that all %s voters it did not expect voted Studentska lista.", fmt_n(round(extra_voters, -3))))
```

<div class="callout callout-result">
**Result.** Even in this deliberately extreme scenario, in which the entire turnout surprise consists of *Studentska* voters, the electorate Ipsos was trying to measure would have had *Studentska lista* at `r fmt_pct(100 * p_turnout[1])` and *Ujedinjena Srbija* at `r fmt_pct(100 * p_turnout[2])`, still a clear Studentska lead and still far from Ipsos's 40.0 / 47.4. The probability of Ipsos's result under this adjusted population is `r fmt_log10p(g_turn["log10_p_G"])`. The turnout *surplus* is not the explanation.

One caveat belongs here. Turnout can also shift a poll without changing the total: if many people who told Ipsos they would vote for *Ujedinjena Srbija* stayed at home, while an equal number who had said they would *not* vote turned out for *Studentska lista*, aggregate turnout is unchanged but the electorate Ipsos modelled is not the one that voted. Such *gross* flows are a failure of the pollster's likely-voter model rather than of sampling, and they are not observable from the outside; to produce Ipsos's picture they would have to involve several hundred thousand voters swapping places. We treat this, together with the handling of undecided respondents, under Scenario 4 and under non-sampling error in the conclusions.
</div>

## Scenario 3: both together

Combining the two, an extreme turnout assumption *and* a late swing, how large would the swing still have to be?

```{r combined}
t_05_comb <- uniroot(function(t) swing_log10p(t, p_from = p_turnout) - log10(0.05), c(0, 1))$root
voters_05_comb <- t_05_comb * (p_turnout[1] - p_ips_A[1]) * sum(votes_t)
```

<div class="callout callout-result">
**Result.** With the extreme turnout assumption already in place, a further **`r fmt_n(round(voters_05_comb, -3))` voters** (`r fmt_pct(100 * voters_05_comb / sum(votes_t), 1)` of the remaining ballots) would still have had to move to *Studentska lista* in three days to bring Ipsos's result up to a 5% probability. The two electorate-side explanations do not add up to an explanation.
</div>

## Scenario 4: undecided voters

Ipsos's percentages describe only the respondents who named a list. Section 6 suggested that this "decided" base was perhaps `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * n_primary * deff_full / ipsos_n)` of the sample, leaving roughly a fifth undecided. Suppose Ipsos's decided respondents were a perfect picture of the decided electorate, and that the entire gap arose because the undecided voters, once they made up their minds, voted very differently. How lopsided would their choice have had to be?

If a share *u* of eventual voters was undecided at the time of the poll, the final result is (1 − *u*) × (Ipsos's decided picture) + *u* × (how the undecided voted). Knowing the final result and Ipsos's picture, we can solve for the third term.

```{r undecided}
undec <- purrr::map_dfr(c(0.20, 0.25, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50), function(u) {
  q <- (p_rik_A - (1 - u) * p_ips_A) / u          # how the undecided must have voted
  tibble::tibble(u = u,
                 `Studentska lista` = 100 * q[1], `Ujedinjena Srbija` = 100 * q[2],
                 `Manjinske liste` = 100 * q[3], Other = 100 * q[4])
})
undec |>
  dplyr::mutate(`Undecided share` = fmt_pct(100 * u, 0), .keep = "unused", .before = 1) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(-`Undecided share`, ~ gsub("-", "−", sprintf("%.0f%%", .x)))) |>
  kable_report(caption = "Table 16. Scenario 4: how the undecided voters would have had to split for Ipsos's decided picture to have been exactly right. Negative values are impossible.")
```

<div class="callout callout-result">
**Result.** If a fifth of the eventual voters were undecided when Ipsos polled, no split works at all: they would have had to vote *more than 100%* for *Studentska lista*. With a quarter undecided they would have had to vote **`r sprintf("%.0f%%", undec[["Studentska lista"]][2])` for *Studentska lista*** and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", undec[["Ujedinjena Srbija"]][2])` for *Ujedinjena Srbija*; with a third undecided, `r sprintf("%.0f%%", undec[["Studentska lista"]][3])` and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", undec[["Ujedinjena Srbija"]][3])`. And in every row up to about 40% undecided the small lists come out *negative*: because Ipsos put the small lists and invalid ballots too high as well, no split of the undecided voters can reconcile the whole vector; they would have had to take votes *away* from the small lists, which is impossible. Undecided voters do break unevenly in real elections, and a late-deciding bloc favouring a protest movement is entirely plausible; a bloc of this size voting almost unanimously is not what the literature describes. This scenario is also, like the previous two, the most generous reading possible: it assumes Ipsos's decided respondents were a perfect sample, with zero sampling error of their own.
</div>

# Summary and conclusions

## What we did

1. **Collected both records.** Ipsos's final estimate of 22 October 2026 (n = 3,624; *Ujedinjena Srbija* 47.4%, *Studentska lista* 40.0%, with 95% intervals of about ±2.1 points, commissioned by the *Ujedinjena Srbija* list) and RIK's count as of 31 October 2026 (8,339 of 8,392 polling stations; *Studentska lista* `r fmt_pct(scheme_a$rik_pct[1])`, *Ujedinjena Srbija* `r fmt_pct(scheme_a$rik_pct[2])`; turnout `r fmt_pct(rik_meta$turnout_pct)`).
2. **Made them comparable.** Both use "all ballots cast" as the base, so no rescaling was needed. We grouped the lists into *Studentska lista*, *Ujedinjena Srbija*, the four *manjinske liste* that entered Parliament, and everything else. Ipsos's error is concentrated in the two large lists, `r sprintf("%.1f", scheme_a$rik_pct[1] - 40)` points too low for *Studentska lista* and `r sprintf("%.1f", 47.4 - scheme_a$rik_pct[2])` points too high for *Ujedinjena Srbija*, with the remaining `r sprintf("%.1f", sum(scheme_a$ipsos_pct[3:4] - scheme_a$rik_pct[3:4]))` points spread as small overestimates across the minor lists, the minority lists and invalid ballots.
3. **Established the effective sample size** from Ipsos's own confidence intervals: about `r fmt_n(n_primary)` decided respondents, the most generous figure the published precision supports.
4. **Computed the probability** of Ipsos's result under the hypothesis that it was a random sample of the actual electorate, in five different ways, including an exact computation that enumerates every possible outcome of the poll, two simulation estimates, and the textbook chi-square approximation.
5. **Stress-tested** the result against every alternative sample size, population definition and base (all ballots versus valid votes).
6. **Quantified** what a late swing, a turnout surprise or a lopsided break of undecided voters would have had to look like to explain the gap.

## What we found

<div class="callout callout-result">
<div class="hero">≈ `r sub(" \\(.*$", "", fmt_log10p(log10_p_exact))`</div>
<div class="hero-sub">the probability that a random sample of the people who voted on 25 October 2026 would produce a result at least as far from the truth as Ipsos's published numbers (exact multinomial test, all `r fmt_n(enum[["n_outcomes"]])` possible outcomes enumerated, four categories, n = `r fmt_n(n_primary)`; every other method and every variant we tried lands between `r fmt_pow(tail_range_all[2])` and `r fmt_pow(tail_range_all[1])`)</div>

- Taken one list at a time, the chance of a random sample putting *Studentska lista* at or below 40.0% when its true share was `r fmt_pct(scheme_a$rik_pct[1], 1)` is `r fmt_log10p(m2$log10_p[1])`; the chance of putting *Ujedinjena Srbija* at or above 47.4% when its true share was `r fmt_pct(scheme_a$rik_pct[2], 1)` is `r fmt_log10p(m2$log10_p[2])`.
- Asking for both at once (*Studentska lista* at or below 40.0% *and* *Ujedinjena Srbija* at or above 47.4%) gives `r fmt_log10p(log10(joint_exact))` exactly. The textbook chi-square approximation gives `r fmt_log10p(gA["log10_p_G"])` with four categories and `r fmt_log10p(gB["log10_p_G"])` with all lists kept separate.
- Among **two million** simulated ideal random polls from the real electorate, **none** came close to Ipsos's combination, under any of the definitions of "close" we tried.
- The conclusion is unchanged for any sample size from 1,500 to 3,624, whether or not Kosovo i Metohija and the diaspora are removed from the population to match Ipsos's sampling frame, and whether the comparison is made on all ballots or on valid votes only: the probability never rises above about `r fmt_pow(max(c(sens_n[["G test (Scheme A)"]], g_valid["log10_p_G"], gB_valid["log10_p_G"])))`.
- By Ipsos's **own** published margins of error, the true *Studentska lista* share lay `r sprintf("%.1f", own$outside_by[1])` points outside the top of its 95% interval, `r sprintf("%.0f", abs(own$z_own[1]))` of its own standard errors from its estimate.
- To make Ipsos's result an ordinary 1-in-20 unlucky draw, about **`r fmt_n(round(voters_05, -3))` voters** would have had to move to *Studentska lista* in the three days between fieldwork and election day; even if every one of the `r fmt_n(round(extra_voters, -3))` unexpected extra voters had voted *Studentska*, a further `r fmt_n(round(voters_05_comb, -3))` would still have had to move. If a quarter of voters were undecided at the time of the poll, they would have had to vote `r sprintf("%.0f%%", undec[["Studentska lista"]][2])` for *Studentska lista*, and even then the small-list excess remains unexplained.
</div>

```{r words}
# the headline exponent in words (short scale, as used in English; long scale, as used in Serbian)
pow_words <- function(l10) {
  # the number 1/p written as  lead × 10^e, then named: e.g. 3 × 10^36 = "three undecillion"
  e <- floor(-l10); lead <- round(10^(-l10 - e)); if (lead == 10) { lead <- 1; e <- e + 1 }
  grp <- e %/% 3; mult <- lead * 10^(e %% 3)                      # mult in 1..900
  short_names <- c(`10` = "nonillion", `11` = "decillion", `12` = "undecillion", `13` = "duodecillion")
  # Serbian forms: singular (1), paucal (2–4), plural (5+)
  long_names  <- list(`10` = c("kvintilion", "kvintiliona", "kvintiliona"), `11` = c("kvintilijarda", "kvintilijarde", "kvintilijardi"),
                      `12` = c("sekstilion", "sekstiliona", "sekstiliona"), `13` = c("sekstilijarda", "sekstilijarde", "sekstilijardi"))
  if (!as.character(grp) %in% names(short_names)) return(sprintf("one in a %d followed by %d zeros", lead, e))
  en_small <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine")
  en_tens  <- c("ten", "twenty", "thirty", "forty", "fifty", "sixty", "seventy", "eighty", "ninety")
  en_mult  <- if (mult < 10) en_small[mult] else if (mult < 100) en_tens[mult / 10] else paste(en_small[mult / 100], "hundred")
  sr_small <- c("", "dva", "tri", "četiri", "pet", "šest", "sedam", "osam", "devet")
  sr_tens  <- c("deset", "dvadeset", "trideset", "četrdeset", "pedeset", "šezdeset", "sedamdeset", "osamdeset", "devedeset")
  sr_hund  <- c("sto", "dvesta", "trista", "četiristo", "petsto", "šeststo", "sedamsto", "osamsto", "devetsto")
  sr_mult  <- if (mult < 10) sr_small[mult] else if (mult < 100) sr_tens[mult / 10] else sr_hund[mult / 100]
  sr_form  <- if (mult == 1) 1 else if (mult %% 10 %in% 2:4 && !(mult %% 100 %in% 12:14)) 2 else 3
  sr_name  <- long_names[[as.character(grp)]][sr_form]
  sprintf("**one in %s %s** (a %d followed by %d zeros; in the long-scale naming used in Serbian and most of continental Europe, *%s*)",
          en_mult, short_names[as.character(grp)], lead, e, trimws(paste(sr_mult, sr_name)))
}
```

## What it means, and what it does not

**Sampling error alone cannot account for the gap.** The hypothesis that Ipsos's published numbers are what a random sample of actual voters would produce, with chance as the only source of discrepancy, is rejected by every method: the exact probability is about `r sub(" \\(.*$", "", fmt_log10p(log10_p_exact))`, that is, roughly `r pow_words(log10_p_exact)`. Depending on the definition of "at least as far from the truth", on the test used and on the treatment of invalid ballots, the figure moves between `r fmt_pow(tail_range_all[2])` and `r fmt_pow(tail_range_all[1])`; at this depth a few powers of ten change nothing. For a sense of scale: picking one specific star at random from all the roughly 10<sup>24</sup> stars in the observable universe is a 1-in-10<sup>24</sup> event, and that is about `r fmt_pow(-24 - log10_p_exact)` times *more* likely than Ipsos's result under random sampling. No reasonable choice of sample size, population definition, base or test statistic changes that conclusion. Ipsos's own stated precision leads to the same conclusion without any modelling on our part.

**What the numbers do not establish on their own is the *cause*.** Several candidate explanations remain, and statistics alone cannot pick between them, nor rule out a combination; the evidence in this document bears on each as follows:

- *A genuine late swing.* Possible in principle, and flagged by Ipsos itself as a caveat; but it would have had to involve some `r fmt_n(round(voters_05, -3))` voters moving to the student list within 72 hours, among them roughly one in `r sprintf("%.0f", 1 / (from_us(t_05) / (p_rik_A[2] * rik_meta$ballots + from_us(t_05))))` of all *Ujedinjena Srbija* supporters, a movement several times larger than the late swings documented in comparable elections, and one that no other evidence from those three days suggests.
- *Differential turnout.* Ruled out as a sufficient explanation *in its net form*: even the most extreme assumption about the unexpected extra voters leaves the gap essentially intact. Gross flows (intending voters staying home while others turned out) cannot be assessed from outside; they belong under non-sampling error below.
- *Undecided voters.* A quarter of the electorate undecided and then voting `r sprintf("%.0f%%", undec[["Studentska lista"]][2])` for one list would reconcile the two big numbers; nothing reconciles the small-list excess. A real but modest contribution is plausible; a full explanation is not.
- *Non-sampling error* (telephone coverage, non-response, concealment of intention, mode and house effects, likely-voter modelling, weighting; see [total survey error](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_survey_error)). This is the explanation that the test cannot address directly, and every poll carries some of it. What the test does establish is its required size: a non-sampling bias large enough to explain Ipsos's numbers would have to move the two large lists by 13 and 8 points, far beyond what the polling literature documents for final pre-election polls with fieldwork three days before the vote. Ipsos's election-night projection with CeSID was accurate to within a few tenths of a point, but that projection rested on counted ballots at sampled polling stations, not on interviews, so it does not share the pre-election survey's sources of error and does not by itself tell us how large those could have been.
- *Misrepresentation of the published numbers.* The data are consistent with it, exactly as they are consistent with a sufficiently large version of each explanation above; the test cannot separate them. The fact that the poll was commissioned by one of the contestants is a reason to ask for transparency, not evidence of intent, and this document makes no claim about intent.

The defensible public statement is therefore: **Ipsos's final pre-election numbers cannot have arisen from random sampling error. What remains is some combination of a late swing far larger than any for which there is independent evidence, a turnout or undecided-voter shift of a size the literature does not describe, a methodological bias far larger than final pre-election polls ordinarily carry, and the published numbers not reflecting what the survey measured.** This document cannot distinguish among these, nor between any of them and misreporting. Doing so requires what a probability calculation cannot supply: Ipsos's raw data, its weighting scheme, its likely-voter model, and its treatment of undecided respondents.

## Caveats

- RIK's results used here are **preliminary** (`r fmt_n(rik_meta$stations_done)` of `r fmt_n(rik_meta$stations_total)` polling stations, snapshot of `r rik_meta$snapshot`), and they are taken as the truth throughout. The outstanding `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (1 - rik_meta$stations_done / rik_meta$stations_total))` of polling stations cannot move the national shares by more than a few tenths of a point. Re-knitting this document with the final figures entered in Section 3 will update every computed number automatically.
- The effective sample size is inferred from Ipsos's published intervals, not stated by Ipsos. The sensitivity analysis shows the conclusion is insensitive to it. The counts "out of `r fmt_n(n_primary)`" are a construction that matches the precision of Ipsos's intervals, not interviews Ipsos actually conducted.
- The headline figure is computed exactly, by enumeration, and carries no simulation error. The chi-square figures are asymptotic approximations and are read as orders of magnitude; Pearson's chi-square is reported for completeness but is known to be unreliable this far into the tail. The importance-sampling estimate is reported only to document that, with a proposal centred on Ipsos's numbers, it undercounts the tail by a factor of about `r sprintf("%.0f", 10^(log10_p_exact - log10_p_is))` (its runs spread over `r sprintf("%.1f", diff(is_spread))` in the exponent, which understates its true error).
- Ipsos's percentages are published to one decimal place; converting them to counts introduces errors of up to about one respondent per category, which is immaterial in Scheme A but a reason to treat the smallest Scheme B cells as indicative only.
- Ipsos's assumed 2.5% invalid share is not a sampled quantity; Section 8 shows the effect of removing it from the comparison (a few powers of ten, conclusion unchanged).
- Minority lists are defined here as the four that won seats. Other lists representing national minorities (e.g. *Zukorlić (SPP)*) are in the "Other" category in both sources, so the comparison is consistent.
